full_judgment:
3. These two appeals arise out of the same judgment of the High Court Division and leave was granted to consider the question of interpretation of section 87(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and whether the High Court Division was correct in holding that the plaintiffs are owners of the riparian land by purchase from the original riparian owner and the suit lands being accreted to their land, they are entitled to get the suit lands as they have stepped into the shoes of the original riparian owners. 

 9. Facts may be stated briefly: Plaintiffs case was that the land described in Schedule 1 of the plaint comprises a portion of bed of the river Dakatia. The river gradually silted up the land of schedule No. 1 of the plaint and thus this land was accretion to the adjoining upper land of the raiyati including the plaintiffs who have been in possession of the entire second schedule lands by growing boro crops for more than 12 years. His contention is that under section 87 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the second schedule are to be considered as accession and increment to the plaintiffs raiyati land. On the advice of the local Tahsildar, plaintiffs filed a petition to defendant No. 2 for assessment of rent for the second schedule land in the Settlement Case No. 69 of 1962-63 but the defendant No. 2 assessed the rent for 2'00 acres of land at an annual rent to Tk. 12/50 paisa out of 5.00 acres of land of the second schedule though the plaintiffs are in possession of the entire second schedule land measuring 5'00 acres. These 2'00 acre of land has been shown in the 3rd schedule. The local Tahsildar in collusion with the defendants started Settlement case No. 12 of 1964-65 for assessment of rent of the remaining land of second schedule which have been shown in the 4th schedule of the plaint in the name of second party defendant quite illegally and without jurisdiction. Plaintiffs case was that the defendant had no land near the 4th Schedule and never possessed 4th Schedule or any part of it. Plaintiffs filed an objection against the settlement to the second party defendant on the ground that it was their accreted land and it cannot be settled with second party defendant. The matter was however, decided exparte and the Additional Deputy Commissioner passed the order of assessment in the name of second party defendant with regard to the settlement and ordered for assessment of rent in the name of second party defendant. This was challenged by the plaintiffs. 

 11. Both the Courts below came to the conclusion that the river Dakatia became a lake as a result of the loop cutting by the WAPDA since 1959 and the river started silting up gradually and it became fit for cultivation. Ext A(1) to A(3) admittedly proved about the loop cutting and the gradual development of the bed of the river into dried land. The plaintiffs themselves prayed for settlement of the land which shows that the plaintiffs were not in possession for the last 20/22 years as claimed. It was found that the land belonged to the Government and the plaintiffs themselves admitted the ownership when they took 2 acres of land for settlement after proper salami. In this view of the matter it was concluded that the plaintiffs could not claim that’s land either under section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or under the provision of section 4 of the Bengal Alluvion and Dilluvion Regulation (XI of 1825). In this view of the matter the trial court and the appellate court below dismissed the suit. 

 12. The High Court Division considered section 87 and its amendment by P.O. 137 of 1972. It was noticed that Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was operative in the District on and from 10th May, 1963. The disputed land reformed after the loop cutting in 1959 and the plaintiffs purchased the disputed land prior to 10th of May, 1963 and it was concluded that the plaintiffs are entitled to the benefit of section 87 before amendment. In this view of the matter the order of assessment of rent in the name of defendants by the Additional Deputy Commissioner in Settlement Case No. 12 of 1964-65 regarding the 4th Schedule and of the plaint was declared as illegal and without jurisdiction and the suit was accordingly decreed. 

 17. Then in 1972 by P.O. 72 the entire section 87 was recast and it said that no such land shall be considered as increment but shall vest absolutely in Government. Again, by P.O. 137 of 1972 the position was altered and it provided that the existing provision shall be renumbered as sub-section (1) and two new sub-sections were added, namely, subsection (2) which says that sub-section (1) shall apply to all lands before or after 28.6.72 but shall not apply to any land so gained if the right of a malik to hold as increment was finally recognised or declared before the promulgation of P.O. 137 of 1972 i.e. 4.11.72 and sub-section (3) which says that all suits concerning such land shall abate and no such claim can be entertained by Court. The above analysis of the evolution of section 87 shows that in 1965 when the suit was filed such gradual accession was considered as in increment to the holding subject to the limitation that it shall not exceed the limit mentioned in section 90 and which again will not apply in the case of a large scale, co-operative farming etc. When the suit was filed in 1963 E.P. Ordinance No. VIII of 1967 was not on Statute book nor had its any retrospective effect. Therefore the gradual accession or artificial or mechanical process due to development work by WAPDA would not deprive the plaintiff from increment to his holding. The Bengal Regulation XI of 1825 (The Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Regulation, 1825) noticed that in consequence of the frequent changes which take place in the channel of the principal rivers and the shifting of the sands which lie in the beds of those rivers, chars or small islands are after thrown up by alluvion in the midst of the stream, or near one of the banks and large portion of land are carried away by an encroachment of the river on one side, whilst accessions of lands are at the same time or in subsequent years, by dereliction of the frequent source of contention and affray. The Governor-General in Council promulgated rule "for the general information of individuals as well as for the guidance of Courts of Judicature" and provided when) the land gained by gradual accession from the recess of a river or of the sea "shall be considered a increment to the tenure of the person to whose land or estate, it is thus annexed" and the 4th proviso says that the chars or small and shallow river belong to the proprietor of the indivisibles on the record and the 5th proviso provides that in cases which are no specifically provided for by the rules contained in this Regulation, the Courts of justice in deciding upon such claims and disputes, "shall be guided by the best evidence they may be able to obtain or established by local usage, if there be any applicable to the case, or if not, by general principles of equity and justice." This shows from the very beginning of the Nineteenth century, it was noticed "law and custom of the country had established rule applicable to such cases" and rules were framed under Regulation 11 of 1825 recognizing such increment "to the tenure of the person to whose land or estate it is thus annexed." 

 18. The plaintiffs case was that he purchase the adjoining land of the original riparian raiyat during the year in 1960-63. The disputed land was reformed after the loop cutting in 1959. The suit was filed in the district of Comilla on 26.10.65. Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act became operative from 10th May, 1963. In this view of the matter the High Court Division correctly observed that the suit land as gained by accession to their adjoining land and the plaintiffs are entitled to a benefit of section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act prior to the amendment.
